lesson.text: Quick memory: how should you land after a jump? (Softly, with bent knees.) Gymnasts land like that too. Today: balances, rolls, and joining moves into a sequence.
A balance is a still shape. Hold it for a count of three: make your body tight and strong, stretch your fingers and toes, and fix your eyes on one spot.
The parts of you that touch the floor are your base. A wide base is steadier: two feet and two hands, far apart, is easier to hold than one foot.
Points and patches: a point is a small part, like a hand or a foot; a patch is a big part, like your back or your tummy. Try a balance on 3 points, then one on 1 patch.
Gymnasts make shapes. A star: arms and legs wide. A tuck: knees hugged to your chest. A straight shape: long and thin. A pike: legs straight, bent at the hips.
Rolls: a log roll is long and straight like a pencil; an egg roll is tucked tight. Roll only on a mat, with space all around you and a grown-up watching.
A sequence joins moves together: a start shape, a balance, a travel (a roll, a jump or steps), another balance, and a finish shape. Link them smoothly and hold the start and the finish still.
Try it in the world: build a balance beam one block wide, high above soft wool blocks, and walk along it without falling. Then make up a 5-move sequence for real, on a mat, and show a grown-up.

exercises.prompt: A balance is a still shape that you hold.
exercises.explain: True: a balance is a shape you hold still, for a count of three.

exercises.prompt: How long should you hold a balance?
exercises.hint: Long enough to show you are in control.
exercises.explain: Hold it still for a count of three, so everyone can see it is controlled.

exercises.hint: Where would it be soft and safe?
choices: on a mat, with space around you
exercises.explain: On a mat, with space all around you and a grown-up watching.

exercises.prompt: Standing on one foot is steadier than standing on two feet.
exercises.hint: Try it: which one wobbles more?
exercises.explain: False: two feet make a wider base, so they are steadier.

exercises.hint: More points on the floor, and further apart, make a wider base.
choices: two feet and two hands, wide apart
exercises.explain: Two feet and two hands, wide apart, make the widest base, so it is the steadiest.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a patch, not a point?
exercises.hint: A patch is a big, flat part of you.
exercises.explain: Your back is a big part: a patch. Toes, fingertips and heels are points.

exercises.prompt: Match each gymnastics shape to what it looks like.
exercises.hint: Picture each shape with your body.
exercises.explain: Star: arms and legs wide. Tuck: knees hugged to your chest. Straight: long and thin. Pike: legs straight, bent at the hips.

exercises.prompt: Tight muscles and eyes fixed on one spot help you hold a balance.
exercises.hint: What do gymnasts do to stay still?
exercises.explain: True: a strong, tight body and eyes on one spot stop you wobbling.

exercises.prompt: Put this gymnastics sequence in order.
exercises.hint: Every sequence begins and ends with a still shape.
exercises.explain: Start shape, balance on 3 points, log roll, balance on 1 patch, finish shape.

exercises.prompt: Tilly wobbles in her one-foot balance. What could help most?
exercises.hint: What did the lesson say keeps you still?
choices: looking at one spot and tightening her middle
exercises.explain: Fixing her eyes on one spot and making her middle tight and strong will steady her.

exercises.prompt: What makes a sequence look smooth?
exercises.hint: Think of moves that flow into each other.
choices: linking the moves without stopping to think
exercises.explain: Smooth sequences link one move straight into the next, practised until you know the order.

exercises.prompt: Sort the body parts: point or patch?
exercises.hint: Is it a small part or a big, flat part?
exercises.explain: Points: a hand, a knee, a foot. Patches: your back, your bottom, your tummy.

exercises.prompt: In an egg roll, you stay tucked tight like a ball.
exercises.explain: True: an egg roll is tucked tight; a log roll is long and straight.

exercises.prompt: Why do gymnasts hold their start and finish shapes still?
exercises.hint: What does a still shape tell the audience?
choices: to show where the sequence begins and ends
exercises.explain: Holding the start and finish still shows clearly where the sequence begins and ends.

exercises.prompt: Sort the balances: steadier, or wobblier?
items: two feet and two hands, wide apart
exercises.hint: A wider base, with more of you touching the floor, is steadier.
exercises.explain: Steadier: two feet and two hands wide apart, lying on your back (a big patch), kneeling on two knees. Wobblier: one foot on tiptoe, or one hand: a tiny base.

exercises.prompt: Match each roll or shape to how you make it.
matches: long and straight, like a pencil
legs straight, bent at the hips
exercises.explain: A log roll is long and straight like a pencil. An egg roll is tucked tight like a ball. A pike has straight legs, bent at the hips. A star has arms and legs wide.
